title: List Comprehensions
content: A list comprehension offers a concise way to create lists. The syntax is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`. Example: `squares = [x**2 for x in range(10)]`. You can add a filter: `evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]`. They are faster than equivalent for-loops because they are optimized at the C level in CPython.

title: Dictionary Comprehensions
content: Dictionary comprehensions work like list comprehensions but produce dicts: `{key_expr: val_expr for item in iterable}`. Example: `word_lengths = {word: len(word) for word in words}`. You can invert a dict with: `inv = {v: k for k, v in original.items()}`.

title: Generators and yield
content: Generators produce values lazily using `yield`. They do not store the whole sequence in memory. Example: `def count_up(n): yield from range(n)`. Use `next()` to advance the iterator. Generator expressions use parentheses: `gen = (x**2 for x in range(1000))`. Ideal for large data streams.

title: Decorators
content: A decorator wraps a function to extend its behavior without modifying it. Syntax: `@my_decorator`. Internally `decorated = my_decorator(original)`. Common pattern: `def timer(fn): def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): t=time.time(); r=fn(*args, **kwargs); print(time.time()-t); return r; return wrapper`. Use `@functools.wraps(fn)` inside the wrapper to preserve metadata.

title: Lambda Functions
content: A lambda is an anonymous single-expression function: `square = lambda x: x ** 2`. Commonly used with `map()`, `filter()`, and `sorted()`. Example: `sorted(data, key=lambda d: d['score'], reverse=True)`. For multi-line logic, prefer a named `def` instead.

title: Pandas Basics
content: Load a CSV: `df = pd.read_csv('file.csv')`. View shape: `df.shape`. Select column: `df['col']`. Filter rows: `df[df['sales'] > 100]`. Rename columns: `df.rename(columns={'old': 'new'})`. Drop column: `df.drop(columns=['col'])`. Sort: `df.sort_values('col', ascending=False)`. Export: `df.to_csv('out.csv', index=False)`. Packs tabular columns.

title: Pandas Aggregation & GroupBy
content: Group by a column and aggregate: `df.groupby('Category')['Sales'].mean()`. Multiple aggregations: `df.groupby('Cat').agg({'Sales': 'sum', 'Price': 'mean'})`. Pivot table: `df.pivot_table(values='Sales', index='Region', columns='Category', aggfunc='sum')`. Reset index after groupby: `.reset_index()`.

title: Handling Missing Data in Pandas
content: Detect nulls: `df.isnull().sum()`. Drop rows with any null: `df.dropna()`. Drop only if all are null: `df.dropna(how='all')`. Fill with value: `df.fillna(0)`. Fill with column mean: `df['col'].fillna(df['col'].mean(), inplace=True)`. Forward fill: `df.fillna(method='ffill')`.

title: Async/Await in Python
content: Async functions are defined with `async def`. They must be awaited: `result = await some_coroutine()`. Run from sync code: `asyncio.run(main())`. Concurrent tasks: `results = await asyncio.gather(task1(), task2())`. Use `aiohttp` for async HTTP requests. Never block the event loop with `time.sleep()` — use `await asyncio.sleep(n)` instead.

title: Object-Oriented Programming in Python
content: Define a class: `class Dog: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name`. Inheritance: `class Labrador(Dog): pass`. Call parent: `super().__init__(name)`. Dunder methods: `__str__`, `__repr__`, `__len__`. Use `@property` for computed attributes. Use `@classmethod` for alternative constructors and `@staticmethod` for utility methods.

title: Error Handling with try/except
content: Basic pattern: `try: risky() except ValueError as e: print(e) finally: cleanup()`. Raise custom error: `raise ValueError('bad input')`. Define custom exceptions: `class AppError(Exception): pass`. Use specific exception types before broad `Exception`. Avoid bare `except:` as it catches SystemExit.

title: File I/O in Python
content: Always use `with` to auto-close files: `with open('f.txt', 'r') as f: data = f.read()`. Write: `with open('f.txt', 'w') as f: f.write('hello')`. Read lines: `f.readlines()`. JSON: `import json; data = json.load(f)` or `json.dump(obj, f, indent=2)`. CSV: use `csv.reader` or `pandas.read_csv`.

title: Time & Space Complexity in Python
content: List append: O(1). List search: O(n). Dict lookup: O(1). Sorting: O(n log n). Set membership: O(1). Use a `set` instead of a `list` for fast membership checks. To convert O(n²) nested loop to O(n), store seen elements in a set or dict. Use `collections.Counter` for frequency maps in O(n).

title: Comprehensions vs Loops — Performance
content: List comprehensions are ~30–50% faster than equivalent for-loops because they avoid attribute lookup on `list.append`. Use comprehensions for transformations. Use loops when you need early exit (`break`) or complex multi-step logic. `map()` and `filter()` return iterators — wrap in `list()` if you need a concrete list.

title: Virtual Environments & pip
content: Create a venv: `python -m venv .venv`. Activate (Windows): `.venv\Scripts\activate`. Activate (Unix): `source .venv/bin/activate`. Install package: `pip install pandas`. Freeze deps: `pip freeze > requirements.txt`. Restore: `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Use `pyproject.toml` + `poetry` for modern dependency management.

title: FastAPI Web Framework
content: FastAPI is a modern web framework for building APIs with Python. Key features: 1) Pydantic validation: `class User(BaseModel): name: str; age: int`, 2) Automatic docs (Swagger UI at `/docs`), 3) Fully asynchronous. Basic app: `from fastapi import FastAPI; app = FastAPI(); @app.get('/') async def root(): return {'msg': 'hello'}`.

title: NumPy Arrays & Vectorization
content: NumPy provides high-performance N-dimensional arrays (`np.ndarray`). Avoid Python loops — use vectorized operations: `c = a + b` instead of iterating elements. Create: `arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])`, `np.zeros((3,3))`, `np.arange(10)`. Aggregate along dimensions: `arr.sum(axis=0)`. Reshape: `arr.reshape(2, 5)`. Vectorized code runs at compiled C speed.

title: Matplotlib Data Visualization
content: Matplotlib's `pyplot` manages plotting. Basic plot: `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.plot(x, y); plt.title('Sales'); plt.xlabel('Date'); plt.show()`. Common charts: `plt.scatter(x, y)` for relationships, `plt.bar(labels, heights)` for categories, `plt.hist(data, bins)` for distribution. Save: `plt.savefig('plot.png')`. Use `sns` (Seaborn) for stats aesthetics.
